 One immediate stimulus may have been an article in the Quarterly Review xvi (October 1816)
1–27 (see especially pp. 10–1), reviewing Thomas Legh, Narrative of a Journey in Egypt and
the Country beyond the Cataracts (1816). This article mentions all of the important recurring
details in descriptions of the statue of Osymandias, including the inscription, together with
reflections on the best-known traveller’s accounts (including those of Pococke and Denon). The
Quarterly article definitely seems to be the main source for Horace Smith’s sonnet quoted above,
and the two poems seem very likely to have shared the same occasion, as they both oddly spell
‘Ozymandias’ with a ‘z’ rather than an ‘s’; no other known source does this. Other possible imme-
